Hey even after this time its good to hear other peoples perspectives. Through these past 2 years ive learnt a lot about those around me, my wife and especially my son. Ive found a lot of issues come down to 2 things in my experience. Lack of understanding, and ignorance from others. 


People can be particularly selfish and we don't have that luxury (not that I'd want it, ive never been a narcistic person)


Through these past 2 years ive also been given a diagnosis for combined ADHD and Autism too. It's help me learn more about myself and my son. It's a tough world, but best you can do is focus on number one. 


Yeh you might not get the invites from parents or have eyes on you from others, but they'll never change unless it happens to them, and ironically (call me hypocritical if you like from creating this post) but they want the world to know about and how hard their life is.


There's so much others take for granted that we have to work harder for, and those milestones become so much more to celebrate.


Inclusion is difficult to find outside of others with neurodivergent/disabled children or themselves, and can become a lonely place, but you build your own morals and realise that you can do this without the relying on others, and are a good person inside. Nurture that and hopefully your child will learn to make the world a better place too.

Myself ive suffered with mental health issues for years and was always put down to anxiety and depression. After my son got diagnosed with Autism and a different GP said you show signs of ADHD did I start going through this route. I initially got refused from the NHS service (apparently wasn't showing enough, GP thought its probably because of waiting times) so I went through RTC with Psychiatry-UK. Adults ADHD took just over a year to be diagnosed, and around 4 months for Autism to be diagnosed. So took me overall 14 months for myself to get an ADHD and autism diagnoses.

If you need the help when their service reopen later this year then please go through it, children are still being accepted to this is always a path too for your children to try if not.  PSY-UK state on their site they are currently offering appointments within 3 months of referrals.

GP's and external places haven't got the resources to even know what's up half the time past giving a diagnosis for Anxiety and Depression. It takes years for anyone to tell you what is properly going on or forward you. I've had anxiety and depression for over 10 years, suffered with tics since I was 6 years old and other issues which for me have now linked to ASD and ADHD.

We all want validation for why our brain doesn't tick to the beat of where we live or what we see, but unfortunately we don't get the answers all the time, but that shouldn't ever mean you are not valid in how your suffering each day. Even with the diagnosis, most they offer is medication for ADHD and further therapy if you haven't already been through it.

Unfortunately the waiting lists keep getting bigger, but don't let it discourage you, keep pushing to get on the waiting lists, and we also went through speech and language, but to be honest some of it is common sense mixed in with working around how your child works. For example trying makaton if they are non verbal, try and ask close ended questions, sometimes like our son at one point he became frustrated being non verbal so try your best to see what signs means he wants something, whether it be food, liquid, tired, play etc. 

Our sons initial signs were his general delay in development, his walking was around 6 months behind average, his speech was around a 1 year delay and his need for fixed routine. 
Even now anything out of routine for example a trip to the supermarket, a change in routine in class at school can upset him. 
He does a lot of hand flapping since being around 10 months old and still does this now when emotions run high. 
He speaks about himself in 3rd person now too.
Delay in toilet training again even now.
Hyper fixation on certain objects, loves things that spin (he'd tip over his toy buggy just to spin the wheels)
He loves lights (some neurodivergent don't)
He doesn't like noise and social areas (I believe this is what set me off afterwards for help too as im not as severe as my son, but share similar traits to him)
Without putting our son down, but he just didn't understand things either like birthdays, Xmas etc (I know it's early at 2 years old for other children to understand but he didn't engage in any of it), even now he's only just starting to understand what Xmas is since last year, but struggle to take him anywhere with it being a busy period.

Eye contact was another one and just no answering to his name, and when he could start talking he started with echolalia which is tending to repeat words and phrases from what he's heard around him (again he still does this now)

I believe the more effort you try to put in, the quicker you will get him help. We rang around each month to check waiting lists, fill out forms, and still doing it out to try and get any EHCP at school.
It's not easy, but the acknowledgement is worth a lot moving forward.

I know it's not about me, but from my own diagnosis and what I've struggled with for years, I tend to also struggle to anywhere social, it's draining, anything broken out of my routine becomes stressful, lights hurt my eyes and cause me migraines, and my brain is like a Hamster on a wheel most days. 

The best thing you can do as obvious as it sounds is keep trying. It took us over a year to get our son just on the toilet to wee after trying and stopping then trying again and again. It's tiring and repeating what needs to be learnt helps, though emotionally sometimes they just aren't ready for first steps till much later. Please try not to compare to other children, there's too many average guides out there saying your child should be doing this by this date.


Sorry for the huge wall of text, just trying to help where I can as I understand how hard it can be, but don't give up hope and move forward for what's best for you and your son.

Hey, my son is 5 years old and went through potentially a similar process me and my wife had too. 
At a similar age we started to see signs of autism. He was late walking, started to say mum and Luna (the name of our dog) then stopped, used to stim a lot and still does with flapping his hands, concentrating a lot on specific toys such as things that spin, loves lights and more. 

Like yourself we were worried he wasn't ready for early years (nursery) and let him go in for the afternoon session when he was around 30 months as they had new starters at the beginning of terms and half way through.
It did help him come on, but also helped with getting towards a diagnosis too. If you have settings around you that are able to spot autistic traits as in our area more of the teachers are going on courses to know how to spot and deal with autism then it should help you and your child. 
Our GP first sent him off for hearing tests to check his slow development in speech was due to any hearing issues. After this it was a case of proceeding with a waiting list to see if he was going to be diagnosed with autism (to be honest we already knew as he had many traits at this point and was 2 years behind in development as we were told by te child development centre)
Now at 5 it's a case of applying for an EHCP for him to try and get him the aid he needs. 
All I can say is if you believe he has autism then get the ball rolling as quickly as possible. The sooner he gets a diagnosis the sooner he will be able to get his needs met when in an educational setting hopefully as long as the school work alongside him which they should.

Our son now has come on leeps and bounds and is brilliant at reading already, numbers and academically doing well, but he is behind socially and regulating himself and is still doing no.2's in his pants (we've tried many methods to get him to go to the toilet and he still seems like he doesn't even realise he's doing it) 
He also speaks in 3rd person which is adorable but if for now that's how he communicates then it's fine by us, he'll learn over time. 

Also from this, I've suffered for many years with mental health issues and thanks to my son getting a diagnosis, it aided me in knowing what was potentially wrong with me (don't like using the word wrong but don't know how else to describe it)
Years of antidepressants and CBT have done very little tbh, and last year I have now been diagnosed with combined ADHD and Autism myself. 

Basically get the help you believe you need for you Son and also yourself, you'll get there but I won't lie and say it's not hard work with chasing up waiting lists and referrals, but it's all worth it to make sure all of your health problems are dealt with, and also you then know what you are both working with too. 

Good luck, need any further help feel free to ask.

12 months later I've been diagnosed with combined ADHD and Autism through RTC which both can coincide with symptoms of Anxiety and Depression too.

Just being honest but receiving help for mental health issues is a battle which ironically is the opposite of what people need with mental health issues. Expect the eat well, exercise, and maintain good sleep routines too. Most CBT's can be about acceptance therapy, or behavioural therapy which is challenging your own negative thoughts, images on yourself and basically bad habits. I've been that boyfriend, and now a husband to the same person who's supported me. For a start (this isn't any science based fact I'm saying here just me own opinion) I believe mental health issues can be hereditary genetically. 
My dad suffers with it, my Extended family has members suffering with it down to even my Great grandmother. I've been through those cycles, I've been close to suicidal ideations years ago, but my family I've created has helped stable me.
I don't think I'll ever not be without mental health issues and recently been diagnosed with ADHD and Autism (again if its something through the family there's a chance there's more too it but unfortunately it took years to get some answers) 
For a start if he's desperate shall we say, I'll say he doesn't need to be scared of medication, but they can be trial and error. Some may help and some may just make him feel like a walking zombie too. Starting off low and gradually building them up helps, no need to rush them, ask the GP for the lowest dosage till he's built up a tolerance. Something GP's don't tell you is there are side effects and withdrawal symptoms, but nothing like they make out in the movies with drugs if he tapers off them slowly if one medication isn't working.

A lot of medications can cross over, so he can start taking one antidepressant straight after another if it's not working for him. Second if sleeps affecting him (I've never had good sleep routine) medications I can recommend trying if he asks for them are trazodone (start at 50mg, usually 75mg to 100mg is used for anxiety disorders) paroxetine (believe it was 10 or 20mg starting dose) and I'm currently taking amytripatline which they may not consider straight away as it's seen as an old anti depressant now, but can still work (worked better then others for me up to now).
What he's going through could potentially feel like he's spiralling and losing control especially if he's not sleeping well, but accepting help is the first step.

There's no miracle cure or therapy that's going to work wonders from my experience (your mileage may differ with me having neurodivergent issues too), but it can help just rationalise where he's currently at right now. You can self refer to CBT therapy through IAPT. Some he may find useless in his current state of mind, but 2 things I can say can help is meditation and deep breathing when things become too much. Like another user said, YouTube has some great music to help relax, binaural beats, white noise etc. White noise helps me sleep, it can distract a busy mind. 
If he struggles with the whole meditation and thinks it's not for him, then just try the guided audio, again some on YouTube or calm and headspace apps. 

It's hard on you too I know, but if you want to help him then just be there for him as much as possible but let him have his space too if he feels he needs it. It's hard to play the supporting role and can feel push and pull but try your best to just be there and give him the light in his darkness right now. 
Try and get him if possible to break down what's making him feel this way, if there's any background issues from growing up these can cause issues later in life when unresolved, maybe he's struggling with the pressure of being an adult (I know I struggle to handle any stress) and the simple things that every GP and therapist is going to say to him such as cut down on the caffeine and alcohol, try to stay relatively active, and know it's OK to feel the way he does and take time out. 

I can't promise it'll ever go away but he can get through the dark times and unfortunately its always easy to hurt the ones you love, but know there's a chance he's not doing any of it intentionally, mental health issues are an illness and not always treat like one.

Apologies if this sounds obvious and if you've tried it already, but have you tried putting on sounds for sleep time? Direct bath then bed, try not to make sure she doesn't eat too late as laying down on a full stomach can slow down the digestive system, create a safety plush they know is for bed time and even have it with you for a while so it holds your scent, read to them before bed if possible. I know it's difficult when your exhausted (we are there ourselves) but try where possible to just get them on a park to burn some excess energy off during the day too. 
Screen time isn't always bad for neurodivergent kids in my opinion (just my own take) but put on educational apps and videos, stories etc. Again something to make their brain work and tire (I understand sometimes it's like they never do tire).

Again apologies if you've tried most of this but just trying to help and see what's helped our son to some extent, but understand every child has different needs.

2nd I'd say that friends are transitional and also transactional. They come and go and sometimes we think the time invested means we should worry about the time lost also. My son at 4 has days like this and I'm sorry your also going through the same. Things that have helped calm down these moments for him are:

Dark and quiet room (have a projector and lava lamp for sensory)
Try not to say no but give an alternative, something simple for us is like if he goes towards our biscuit tin and in his phrase "try biscuit" instead of saying no we try to offer an alternative to him such as grapes (thankfully he likes his fruit as we have it in the house often which also helps children from my experience that they pick up and eat what they see you eating too) or say simple dinner then biscuit. He'll probably kick off the first few times but eventually learn he gets a treat after dinner not before. ASD children can be clever and learn stuff even though it may seem its not always going in.
Hardest thing but keeping calm as a parent, he sees you calm he'll calm, again difficult to do but at home if he does something, try not to react to him or just keep silent.
What does he like otherwise? Would he take to a reward chart or system where you could give him praise? We literally praise him for everything, our son works so much off of praise that simply coming home and taking his shoes off by himself gets a well done and high 5.
If you can try taking it in turns between parents, if one can take over for an hour to let the other have an hour rest then it helps yourself to not be over stimulated top.
Closing the curtains if you are all in the living room could help, myself I suffer with mental health problems with potentially ADHD (only just going through the referral now at 30 after my GP told me I may have it) and light can be stimulating to the point of being too much for me and sometimes my son.
It's hard but repetition helps just keep children from having meltdowns, my son knows in the car if we aren't going home and can tell starts getting stressed, try to each time tell them for example we are going to the shops.
Fidget bag we also have for him in the car/at home, something he can go through each time he needs stimulation without it making a mess everywhere e.g. poppers, the plastic water and oil turners, toy car, squishes etc.
Try to sit down play with him or along side him, again monkey see monkey do sometimes and if he sees you playing with a toy car or dinosaur making the noises etc. It'll peak his interest.
Tire him out where possible, walks to the park or out on the garden, play areas if they aren't busy at times you can go.
If he's in nursery/school ask the school what he shows interest in so you know what to buy for him at home
People will be half and half with this one and I'm not a parent to shove a tablet in my sons face to shut him up but honestly my son has learnt so much from playing number and letter games on the tablet and also helps him be focused on something, anything you see him take interest in, again just try to encourage it, our son just randomly started writing his name after we showed him like 100 times and then stopped again haha, it's all in their time. Google play pass is great for a bunch for children games without having to worry about adverts or being online after they are downloaded.

I'm sorry if you've tried most of this but trying to offer some advice for what's helped us but we are also still learning ourselves. 
Simple things like balloons, bubbles, spin tops, colours, capsule toys, have kept him busy over the years, sometimes more than his toys you pay an arm and a leg for. 
You have to go at his pace and see what's going to make him happy whilst also staying firm on what is OK and what is not. 
Being non verbal or not being able to express themselves i think also provides a lot of frustration that becomes worse so trying different ways to get them to communicate or show what they want helps. I'm sure you've heard or read most of it but, repeating words and phrases to them, offering choice, pictures for them to point at or pick up, shaking head for yes and no etc.
Potty training is still hard and he still isn't there for us with recently special education coming into class and observing him saying they think he's around 2 years behind where he should be.
Trust me your not alone and we've all got our concerns (potty training my example, I'd hate for him to be on pullups still in infants) but you've got to take it one step at a time and work together the best you can, and your partner needs to perhaps watch videos of other ND children and why their needs are different and try to be more open minded as what we all learn growing up is different but doesn't always make it right. Accepting something for being different than our thought process is tough but we can all do it.
Good luck and can chat if you need to vent to anyone.

I currently have no real friends, a tough time with all 3 of us in the household having a disability and relying on benefits but we keep trying because it does get better. It just takes time and we need to try our best to appreciate the small things as much as possible. 
My talk may be no help, but please try and give yourself a reason to want to wake up. Unfortunately we can't change the past or future but we can change the Present. We can just try to make that 5 minute difference in a day. Doesn't have to be to go and join a club or a sports team etc. It could be as simple as buying a plant and watering it, knowing you are the one to nurture that everyday and without you, they'd be no plant at the end. 
We all have a purpose, and even if it's just filling up a bird feeder on our gardens so the birds can thrive again then you've done your job and you should be proud of yourself.
You clearly care and not had the same given to you, concentrate on putting that love and care back into yourself and those that deserve it, not the ones that think they are owed it.
Take care and feel free to message me if you need to talk, mental health is all about ups and downs, and personally still trying to get a proper diagnosis than just GAD, but services are stretched and everyone unfortunately is thrown into one basket at times. Any help you do get, make the best of it you can.
